name: esports data APIs
title: Best Esports Data APIs in 2026
summary_line: Esports data APIs deliver match results, player stats, schedules and betting odds as feeds that apps, media sites and sportsbooks can build on.
definition: An esports data API is a programmatic feed of competitive gaming information: fixtures, live scores, rosters, player and team statistics, and in some products odds and settlement. Buyers include media sites, fantasy products, sportsbooks and developers building companion apps. Sources range from official publisher data to community parsers and commercial aggregators.
intro: Anyone building a schedule widget, a stats site or a betting product asks the same two questions: where does the data come from, and what does a request cost? The ten candidates on this list answer differently. Some are commercial feeds sold on quote to sportsbooks, one publishes self-serve prices, a few are free but limited to a single game, and one is a developer gateway into a single publisher's titles. We read vendor pages, documentation indexes and pricing tables, noted what each one says about coverage and licensing, and ranked by how well a small to mid-size product team could actually start. Official and odds-grade sources rank above single-game hobby feeds when the facts support it.

criteria.heading: Title coverage and depth
criteria.text: Count the games and the layer of detail. A schedule feed that lists results is a different product from one with 350 data points per match. Vendors here range from five flagship titles to a dozen and more, and a few go no further than one game. Check that your titles are named, not implied.

criteria.heading: Data provenance and licensing
criteria.text: Official data from a publisher or league carries rights that scraped statistics do not. Look for the words official, licensed or integrity in the vendor copy, and read restrictions on use: one vendor bars betting-related usage from its stats plans, while others sell only to operators.

criteria.heading: Access model and cost
criteria.text: Self-serve keys with published rate limits suit a prototype; quote-only contracts suit a sportsbook. Ask whether a free tier or trial exists, how rate limits are counted, and whether a per-game fee applies. Hidden pricing is common in this niche, so plan a sales call into your timeline.

criteria.heading: Delivery and tooling
criteria.text: REST and GraphQL are the norm, but push delivery over a socket matters for live odds. Widgets, white-label sites and documentation quality decide how fast a small team ships. Check for an interactive docs site and for helpers such as champion, hero or map lookups.

market_notes: Pricing transparency is rare here. Of ten products, PandaScore alone prints figures (stats plans from 400 euros and 1000 euros per game per month, with a free tier at 1000 requests per hour). Five more, GRID, Oddin.gg, Sportradar, GameScorekeeper and OddsMatrix, sell on quote or demo, with OddsMatrix adding a one-month trial. OpenDota is open source, STRATZ is free with a paid STRATZ+ tier, and Riot and Steamworks gate access through applications.

Geography skews European among vendors that name a base: PandaScore in Paris, GRID in Berlin, GameScorekeeper in Aarhus and Sportradar in St. Gallen. The trade-off is between licensed breadth and open access. Commercial feeds give rights, uptime promises and several titles but need a contract, while community feeds cost nothing and cover one game. Teams building for betting should check license terms first, because the cheaper plans often exclude that use.

how_to_choose.title: Pin down the use case and licensing
how_to_choose.text: Decide whether you are showing scores, powering fantasy points or pricing odds. Betting use is the strictest: one self-serve vendor excludes it from its stats plans, and operator-focused vendors sell only through sales. Write the use case into your first email so you are quoted the right product.

how_to_choose.title: List the titles and the data depth you need
how_to_choose.text: Write down the games and the fields, such as live round data, player stats or only results. Compare against the coverage pages. A vendor with twelve titles and results may still lack the per-round fields your widget needs, and a single-game parser may be deeper than any commercial feed.

how_to_choose.title: Prototype on a free key before you sign
how_to_choose.text: Use PandaScore's free plan, OpenDota, STRATZ or a Riot developer key to test your schema, then ask a commercial vendor for a trial. Check documentation quality, rate limits and push delivery during the trial, not after the contract.

faqs.q: What is the best esports data API in 2026?
faqs.a: PandaScore is first for most teams: it has a free tier, published stats plans, and covers League of Legends, CS2, Dota 2 and more. GRID is the better pick when official data and a sportsbook-grade contract matter, and GameScorekeeper is stronger when you need a dozen titles through a documented REST API.

faqs.q: Which esports data providers offer official data?
faqs.a: GRID describes itself as an official esports live data platform covering five titles. Oddin.gg offers an official data feed for operators. Riot's developer portal is the publisher's own gateway to its games. Ask each about the leagues and rights behind the feed you want.

faqs.q: Is there a free esports API?
faqs.a: Yes, with limits. PandaScore's free plan allows 1000 requests per hour for schedules and results, OpenDota is open source for Dota 2, and STRATZ is free to use with a GraphQL API. Riot issues developer keys through an application process.

faqs.q: Can I use these APIs for betting?
faqs.a: Not all of them. PandaScore forbids betting-related usage on its stats plans. GRID, Oddin.gg, OddsMatrix and Sportradar are aimed at operators with odds and settlement. Confirm licensing in writing, as rules vary by title and territory.

faqs.q: How much do esports data feeds cost?
faqs.a: Only PandaScore publishes rates: stats plans from 400 euros and 1000 euros per game per month, with a 10% annual discount. The rest quote privately. Budget for a sales cycle and ask whether prices depend on titles, request volume or client type.

faqs.q: What delivery formats do esports APIs use?
faqs.a: GameScorekeeper documents a REST API, STRATZ a GraphQL API and OddsMatrix offers HTTP pull and TCP socket push. Widgets and white-label sites are available from GRID and GameScorekeeper for teams that prefer embeds.

faqs.q: Do I need Steamworks for esports data?
faqs.a: Rarely. Steamworks is Valve's toolset for configuring and running games on Steam, not an esports statistics feed. Use it if you publish a game on Steam; use a data vendor for tournament and match feeds.

tools.name: PandaScore
tools.tagline: Esports data and odds API with a free plan
tools.pricing: Free plan with schedules, results and context data, limited to 1000 API requests per hour. Stats plans from 400€ and from 1000€ per videogame per month, custom plans configured via sliders; annual plans get a 10% discount.
tools.platforms: Web API covering multiple esports titles
features: Static game data for all games
Stats for LoL, CS2 and Dota 2
tools.summary: PandaScore pairs a free tier with published stats plans, so a team can start without a sales call and scale per game.
tools.verdict: PandaScore is the practical first choice. Every account starts on a free plan with schedules, results and context data at 1000 API requests per hour, no credit card needed. Paid stats plans begin at 400 euros and 1000 euros per game per month, with a 10% discount on annual terms, and the feed covers League of Legends, CS2 and Dota 2 plus an odds feed. Published prices let a small team budget before talking to anyone.
tools.weaknesses: Stats plans are not available for betting-related usage, per the pricing page, which closes the door for sportsbook builders on those tiers. Costs are per game, so a multi-title product adds up quickly.
tools.wrong_for: Not for sportsbooks that need licensed live odds on the stats tier; look at GRID or Oddin.gg. Dota 2 hobbyists can start with OpenDota.

sources.fact: All accounts start on a free plan with 1000 API requests per hour, with no credit card required.
Stats plans start from 400€ and 1000€ per videogame per month; annual plans come with a 10% discount.
Customers with a betting-related usage are not permitted to use PandaScore's stats plans.

tools.name: GRID
tools.pricing: Commercial plans by audience (rights holders, sportsbooks, prediction exchanges, media); no prices on the plans page, access starts with a form.
tools.platforms: Data feeds and API, embeddable widgets, for CS2, LoL, Dota 2, VALORANT and Rainbow Six Siege
tools.summary: GRID provides official live data for five flagship titles with widgets, odds and integrity services, sold through commercial plans by audience.
tools.verdict: GRID is the licensed option. It calls itself an official esports live data platform and covers Counter-Strike 2, League of Legends, Dota 2, VALORANT and Rainbow Six Siege, with live data, GRID Odds, widgets and integrity as listed products. The legal entity is GRID eSports GmbH in Berlin, founded in 2018. Plans are split by audience (rights holders, sportsbooks, prediction exchanges, media), which tells a buyer which contract to ask for.
tools.weaknesses: Prices are not published and access starts with a form. Five titles is narrower than some aggregators, and it is built for commercial buyers, so hobby projects will find no self-serve tier.
tools.wrong_for: Skip it for prototypes or a single-game fan site; PandaScore has a free tier and OpenDota is open. If you need a dozen titles, read GameScorekeeper.

sources.fact: GRID is an official esports live data platform for sportsbooks, prediction markets and media.
GRID was founded in 2018 and is headquartered in Berlin.
GRID's plans page offers commercial plans by audience and has no published prices; access starts with a form.

tools.name: GameScorekeeper
tools.tagline: Esports data API with widgets and white-label sites
tools.pricing: Pricing is not published; data packages are sold through contact.
tools.summary: GameScorekeeper covers twelve titles through a documented REST API and adds widgets and white-label websites for media clients.
tools.verdict: GameScorekeeper, founded in 2016 in Aarhus, Denmark, cites more than 75,000 matches and 6,000 tournaments a year. Its coverage page names twelve games, including CS2, League of Legends, Dota 2, Call of Duty, Valorant and Rocket League, and its public documentation lists sports, competitions, stages and fixtures endpoints. Widgets and white-label sites help teams without front-end capacity. That breadth and documentation earns third place.
tools.weaknesses: Pricing is not published; data packages are sold through contact. It sells to businesses in media, fantasy and betting, and nothing opened says whether the data is official or sourced from third parties.
tools.wrong_for: Not for solo developers who want a free key; use PandaScore's free plan. Operators needing odds should compare OddsMatrix or Oddin.gg.

sources.fact: GameScorekeeper says it was founded in 2016 and is headquartered in Aarhus, Denmark.
The coverage page lists Counter-Strike 2, League of Legends, Dota 2, Call of Duty, Honor of Kings, Arena of Valor, Mobile Legends, Wild Rift, Rainbow Six Siege, Valorant, Overwatch and Rocket League.
The public API documentation lists sports, competitions, stages and fixtures endpoints plus LoL champion, Dota 2 hero and CS2 map lookups.

tools.name: Oddin.gg
tools.pricing: Not published on the opened pages; the vendor asks prospects to request a demo.
tools.platforms: Operator-facing odds feed, data feed and widgets
tools.summary: Oddin.gg supplies an odds feed, official data feed, widgets and a BetBuilder to operators, and says 300+ platforms use it.
tools.verdict: Oddin.gg is built around the sportsbook workflow. Its site lists an esports odds feed, an official data feed, widgets, BetBuilder, fast betting content and a casino product, and says more than 300 operators and platforms trust it. The About page gives 2018 as its founding year. For an operator that wants esports markets without building a trading desk, that bundle is the point of the product.
tools.weaknesses: Pricing is not published and the vendor asks prospects to request a demo. Its focus on operators leaves media sites and independent developers outside the target buyer, and the facts do not list titles.
tools.wrong_for: Not for editorial or fan products that need stats only; GameScorekeeper or PandaScore fit better.

sources.fact: Oddin.gg offers esports betting infrastructure for operators, including an odds feed and an official data feed.
Oddin.gg was founded in 2018, according to its About page.
Oddin.gg says it is trusted by 300+ operators and platforms worldwide.

tools.name: OddsMatrix
tools.tagline: Sports and esports odds feed from EveryMatrix
tools.best_for: Bookmakers adding esports to a sports feed
tools.pricing: Pricing is not published; the vendor offers a one-month free trial and agrees packaging with each client.
tools.platforms: Pull API over HTTP and push API over TCP socket
tools.summary: OddsMatrix offers pull and push APIs across 75+ sports and 20+ esports titles, with a one-month free trial.
tools.verdict: OddsMatrix is a general betting feed that includes esports, which suits a bookmaker who wants one integration for football and CS2. The vendor says it covers 20+ esports titles (six based on traditional sports such as FIFA and NBA2k), supports HTTP pull and TCP socket push, and offers a one-month free trial. Being powered by EveryMatrix gives it an operator-side parent. It is fifth because esports is a part of a much larger catalog.
tools.weaknesses: Pricing is not published and packaging is agreed with each client. Esports depth is not described beyond title counts, and nothing indicates player-level stats.
tools.wrong_for: Skip it for esports-only stats products; GRID or PandaScore go deeper. Teams without a sportsbook need no odds feed.

sources.fact: OddsMatrix says it delivers real-time betting odds, scores and settlements for sports and esports with a one-month free trial.
The vendor says it covers 75+ sports and 20+ esports titles, including six based on traditional sports such as FIFA and NBA2k.
The FAQ says clients agree on packaging, request a trial account and connect through PULL (HTTP) and PUSH (TCP socket) APIs.

tools.name: Sportradar
tools.tagline: Sports data, odds and integrity services
tools.best_for: Large operators wanting one global vendor
tools.pricing: Not published on the opened pages; the vendor asks prospects to contact sales.
tools.platforms: APIs and data products for developers and businesses
tools.summary: Sportradar sells sports data APIs, odds, streaming and integrity services from St. Gallen, with documentation at docs.sportradar.com.
tools.verdict: Sportradar calls itself the world's leading sports technology company at the intersection of sports, media and betting. Its imprint names Sportradar AG in St. Gallen, Switzerland, and it documents developer APIs on a public docs site. A large operator that already buys football and basketball data may prefer consolidating esports there. Its Synergy coaching and scouting product and integrity services widen the offer beyond raw feeds.
tools.weaknesses: Pricing is not published and the vendor asks prospects to contact sales. The pages we opened do not list esports titles or depth, so coverage for your game must be confirmed.
tools.wrong_for: Not for small teams without a sales budget; start on PandaScore's free plan. Esports specialists should compare GRID.

sources.fact: Sportradar describes itself as the world's leading sports technology company, at the intersection of sports, media and betting.
Sportradar AG, Feldlistrasse 2, CH-9000 St. Gallen, Switzerland, is named in its imprint.
Sportradar offers sports data APIs for developers, documented at docs.sportradar.com.

tools.name: Riot Developer Portal
tools.pricing: No prices on the portal; access runs through product registration and an application process.
tools.summary: The Riot Developer Portal grants API access to League of Legends, TFT, Valorant, Legends of Runeterra, Riftbound and 2XKO via registration.
tools.verdict: This is the primary source for Riot titles. The portal published by Riot Games, Inc. offers web APIs, API keys, product registration, rate limiting and versioning for League of Legends, Legends of Runeterra, Teamfight Tactics, Valorant, Riftbound and 2XKO. If your product only covers Riot games, building on the publisher's data avoids a middleman. It ranks seventh because it is not a multi-game esports feed.
tools.weaknesses: Access runs through registration and an application process, and the portal shows no prices. It covers only Riot titles, and the facts say nothing about tournament schedules or odds.
tools.wrong_for: Skip it for multi-title coverage; use GameScorekeeper or PandaScore. Dota 2 builders should look at OpenDota.

sources.fact: The Riot Developer Portal gives developers access to Riot game APIs, including League of Legends, TFT and Valorant.
Developers get access through product registration and an application process.
The portal is published by Riot Games, Inc.

tools.name: OpenDota
tools.pricing: Free and open source; the source code is published on GitHub at odota/core.
tools.summary: OpenDota is a free, open source Dota 2 data platform with automated replay parsing and code on GitHub.
tools.verdict: OpenDota gives Dota 2 developers match data and player statistics at no cost. Its repository, odota/core, describes an open source data platform with automated replay parsing, so you can inspect or self-host the code. For a prototype, a Discord bot or an academic project, that openness is hard to beat. It is eighth because it covers one game and offers no commercial guarantees.
tools.weaknesses: Only Dota 2 is covered. The pages opened give no service-level terms, no odds or tournament schedule feed, and no support contract, which matters if your product depends on uptime.
tools.wrong_for: Not for multi-title or betting products; PandaScore or GRID cover several games. Developers wanting GraphQL should try STRATZ.

sources.fact: OpenDota describes itself as open source Dota 2 match data and player statistics.
The OpenDota repository describes it as an open source Dota 2 data platform with automated replay parsing.
OpenDota's home page presents Dota 2 match data and player statistics as its service.

tools.name: STRATZ
tools.tagline: Dota 2 stats site with a GraphQL API
tools.pricing: The website is free to use; a STRATZ+ paid subscription is offered, with no price on the opened pages.
tools.summary: STRATZ offers Dota 2 statistics, match predictions and a GraphQL API, with a free website and a paid STRATZ+ tier.
tools.verdict: STRATZ is a Dota 2 stats website with hero, player and match statistics, leaderboards and AI-powered match predictions, plus a GraphQL API at stratz.com/api. The vendor says the website is free to use, with STRATZ, LLC holding the copyright for 2015 to 2026. A developer who wants flexible queries will like GraphQL. It sits ninth because the data is single-game and the prices for STRATZ+ were not found.
tools.weaknesses: Dota 2 only, and the STRATZ+ price is not on the opened pages. API limits and licensing terms were not read, so check them before you ship.
tools.wrong_for: Skip it for other titles; use PandaScore or the Riot portal. Teams that prefer open code over a hosted service should look at OpenDota.

sources.fact: STRATZ is a Dota 2 stats website offering personalized visualizations, AI-powered match predictions and an API.
STRATZ offers a GraphQL API and a paid STRATZ+ tier.
STRATZ, LLC holds the copyright on the site, which states 2015-2026.

tools.name: Steamworks
tools.tagline: Valve's toolset for operating games on Steam
tools.pricing: Joining requires filling out paperwork and paying a 'small per-app fee'. No revenue-share terms are given, and the page does not say whether Steamworks itself is free to use.
tools.platforms: Steam, with Steam VR, Steam Deck and Remote Play to phones, tablets and TVs mentioned.
tools.summary: Steamworks supplies Steam Workshop, Inventory, matchmaking and Playtest tools, but the pages show no esports statistics feed.
tools.verdict: Steamworks belongs on this list because developers often ask Steam for player and game data. The vendor page describes it as Valve's set of tools and services for configuring, managing and operating games on Steam, with Workshop, Input, Inventory, microtransactions, matchmaking and lobbies. If you publish on Steam, it is the system you will use for your own game. For competition results and schedules, it is not the right source, which is why it ranks last.
tools.weaknesses: Joining requires paperwork and a small per-app fee, and the page gives no revenue-share terms. Nothing in the opened pages describes tournament, match or odds data for third parties.
tools.wrong_for: Not for anyone who needs esports results or odds; use PandaScore, GRID or GameScorekeeper. It is only relevant to Steam publishers.

sources.fact: Steamworks is described on the vendor page as Valve's set of tools and services for configuring, managing and operating games on Steam.
The page says joining requires paperwork and a small per-app fee, and gives no revenue-share terms.
The page lists features including Steam Workshop, Steam Input, Inventory Service, Microtransactions, Matchmaking and lobbies, and Steam Playtest.
